title: Erdős Problem #595: Infinite Graphs and Countable Triangle-Free Decomposition
description: Is there an infinite graph G which contains no K₄ and is not the union of countably many triangle-free graphs? A fundamental question by Erdős and Hajnal about the chromatic structure of infinite graphs. OPEN, $250 prize.

meta.author: Erdős-Hajnal
originalContributions: hasCliqueInfinite: clique predicate using Set.ncard for infinite graphs
isKFreeInfinite, isK4Free, isTriangleFree: forbidden subgraph predicates
erdos595_conjecture: formal statement of the open problem
erdos_595_summary theorem: combines Folkman and C₄-free results
meta.assumptions: 3 axiom(s): folkman_finite_resistance, nesetril_rodl_finite_resistance, c4_free_countable_trees. See Lean source for complete statements.

overview.historicalContext:
This problem originated from Erdős and Hajnal around 1967, exploring the chromatic properties of infinite graphs. It asks whether a 'local' constraint (K₄-free) can coexist with 'global' resistance to decomposition into countably many triangle-free parts.

The finite case is completely solved: Folkman (1970) and Nešetřil-Rödl (1975) proved that for every n ≥ 1, there exists a K₄-free graph that cannot be covered by n triangle-free graphs. The jump to countably infinite covers introduces fundamentally new difficulties.

The problem connects to a broader family of questions about (G₁, G₂) decomposition pairs (Problem #596) and to Folkman numbers (Problem #582). Erdős offered a $250 prize, reflecting the problem's significance and difficulty.
overview.problemStatement:
Is there an infinite graph G which contains no K₄ and is not the union of countably many triangle-free graphs?

**Known Results:**
- For every finite n, there exists a finite K₄-free graph not coverable by n triangle-free graphs (Folkman 1970, Nešetřil-Rödl 1975)
- Every C₄-free graph IS a countable union of trees, hence countably coverable (Erdős-Hajnal)
- The K₄-free countable case remains OPEN
overview.text: Is there an infinite graph G which contains no K₄ and is not the union of countably many triangle-free graphs? A fundamental question by Erdős and Hajnal about the chromatic structure of infinite graphs. OPEN, $250 prize.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines cliques and covering for infinite graphs using Set.ncard. The conjecture is stated as erdos595_conjecture and equivalently as problem595_reformulated. Finite analogues are axiomatized via folkman_finite_resistance and nesetril_rodl_finite_resistance. The contrast result c4_free_countable_trees shows C₄-free graphs are coverable. The summary theorem erdos_595_summary combines Folkman's finite resistance with the C₄-free coverability result.
keyInsights: **Finite resistance does not imply countable resistance**: for each n, K₄-free graphs resist n-covers, but this doesn't extend to countable covers
**C₄-free graphs are coverable**: Erdős-Hajnal showed C₄-free graphs decompose into countably many trees
**Local vs global**: K₄-free is a 'local' constraint; countable non-coverability is 'global'
**Connection to Problem 596**: this is the (K₄, K₃) case of the general (G₁, G₂) decomposition question

**Compactness barrier**: The finite-to-infinite jump fails because compactness arguments don't apply — each finite graph's resistance to n-covers doesn't compose into resistance to ω-covers, a fundamental limitation of finitary Ramsey theory

sections.title: Basic Definitions
sections.mathContext: Infinite graph cliques: $\text{hasCliqueInfinite}(G, k)$ means $G$ contains $K_k$ as a subgraph. $\text{isKFreeInfinite}(G, k) \iff \neg\text{hasCliqueInfinite}(G, k)$.

sections.title: Graph Coverings and Unions
sections.mathContext: $\text{hasCountableTriangleFreeCover}(G)$: $\exists$ countable family $\{G_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of triangle-free subgraphs with $G = \bigcup_i G_i$.

sections.title: The Main Conjecture
sections.summary: erdos595_conjecture: formal statement of the open problem
sections.mathContext: Conjecture: every $K_4$-free graph has a countable triangle-free cover. Formally: $\text{isK4Free}(G) \implies \text{hasCountableTriangleFreeCover}(G)$.

sections.title: Finite Analogues
sections.mathContext: Finite case: every $K_4$-free graph on finitely many vertices has a finite triangle-free cover (Folkman 1970, Nešetřil-Rödl). Proved via Ramsey-type partition.

sections.title: The Infinite Case
sections.mathContext: The finite-to-countable gap: finite covers exist for finite graphs, but extending to countable covers of infinite $K_4$-free graphs is the open problem.

sections.title: Related Results
sections.summary: c4_free_countable_trees axiom: C₄-free graphs are countably coverable
sections.mathContext: Related: $C_4$-free graphs (no 4-cycles) have countable covers by trees (axiomatized). Trees are triangle-free, so this is a stronger structural result for a different forbidden subgraph.

sections.title: Summary
sections.mathContext: Summary theorems: $\text{finite_case_complete}$ packages the solved finite case. $\text{erdos_595_summary}$ records that the infinite case remains open.

conclusion.summary: Problem 595 remains one of the significant open problems in infinite graph theory. The $250 prize reflects its difficulty. The finite analogues are well-understood (Folkman 1970, Nešetřil-Rödl 1975), but the countable case requires fundamentally new ideas. The formalization captures the known results: finite resistance for all n, C₄-free coverability, and the precise conjecture statement.
conclusion.implications: A positive answer would demonstrate a deep structural difference between finite and countable decomposability. A negative answer would establish a powerful compactness-type result for graph coverings.
openQuestions: Does such an infinite K₄-free graph exist?
Can probabilistic or algebraic methods construct an explicit example?
What set-theoretic methods might be applicable?
What is the relationship to the general (G₁, G₂) question (Problem 596)?
